title: What tool (or style) was used to make RPG Maker PNG File for Sideview Actor/Enemies

posts.author: Arrow8
posts.body: Good Evening. I just need some help with terminology to make sure that I can articulate my thoughts clearly when I am ready to generate Sideview PNG images for my project.  Below are three sets of images. Image 1 is from RPG Maker MZ. I like it. I like the level of detail. However, they are just short chibi characters, and I would rather have taller figures.  Image 2 and 3 are traditional 90's 2D graphics. They aren't chibi-looking but do lack the level of detail. To be honest, I haven't found a big image anywhere that has the level of level of cleanliness as image 1.  I do know I need the images to be in 144 X 92 format for tall sprites, and it should show 200% bigger.  Plus, I need to put "$" in the file name to let the RPG maker know that it is a large image, but what is the style? What do I say to people about what I am looking for? Was image one created using a small brush? Is that the reason it has more details? Was it made on a particular canvas?  Let me know if my questions don't make sense; I will try to explain them differently.  Thanks!

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
We don't know for sure what software the original artist used but you can create similar raster images in Photoshop, PAINT.NET, GIMP, etc.
You can also create pixel art in those software if you limit the palette and resolution and use the pencil tool. There are specialized pixel art software like Aseprite or Graphics Gale

posts.author: Zia_
posts.body:
In the end, all of those are pixel art sprites. The amount of possible details is linked to the resolution. The bigger the asset, the more pixels are available to define details. E.g. your 144x92 has a lot more space than the 24x16 next to it.
But the more complex the graphic, the more time (and money, if you want to commission some), is needed to create them.
I think the first sprite was done by drawing the actual Base character on paper or digitally and use it later as a blueprint to do the pixelwork. Same probably with the first example in your category 3. But there are also artists out there working completely different. E.g. I have seen devs using 3D to do the basework of their pixelart.
Shrinking down graphics won't be enough tho, there's still a lot of pixel art to do.
Might work for static battlers for example, but not for Charsets or other animated sprites. They have to be clean. Every pixel has a purpose.

posts.author: Zia_
posts.body:
An additional thought why you might consider the first one to be more detailed than the others. The modern RPG Maker assets tend to use a lot of colors.
Especially older pixel art assets had very limited palettes, so they weren't only smaller, but also limited to as few colors as possible.
Today, those restrictions have aesthetic purposes only, while in the past they were technically mandatory.
Now you can use as many colors as you want, so shading shapes will come with a lot more depth. You could cast light and shadow with 30 different yellow tones.

posts.author: Timeline_man
posts.body:
the original post says "generate" so... I'm assuming you're looking for the terms to put into a generative AI? I would advise against that, even beyond the usual "AI art is bad at being art" which applies, but also because Models don't understand Asset standards. Spritesheets in MV are essentially based on height/width ratios, each cell is a division based on how big the total canvas is (Measured in Pixels). Walking sprites, for example, are divided first into a 2x4 grid of even sections for different sprites, and those are divided into 3x4 grids to signal direction and stepping. I would consult the Help file in the engine for more information on that.
If you were to commission an artist, especially one that works with RM developers frequently (i.e, the ones on this forum), you could request assets in "the style of the MZ RTP" for example, and that would get you a long way to getting the assets you'd want. They'd often also be able to take the meaning for making taller or shorter characters
the MV/MZ style of assets is very detailed pixel art, this is true. And it's largely because it isn't really trying to replicate retro games beyond being low resolution. To my knowledge we don't really have the "style guide" that was used for the assets, though. Keep in mind that it's not exactly an easy style to replicate for most people who don't have a lot of practice doing so.

The size of the battler is dependant on the size of the full image. If you wanted batters that were 144 x 92 as you originally posted, you would arrange them on a sheet proportioned with the battler height. Battlers are 6 cells tall, and 9 cells wide, so the image would be 864 x 828

there is no such distinction in sideview. the way a battler sheet is formatted, each individual frame is 1/6th of the entire file's height and 1/9th of its width.
with character sprites, the $ does as Andar said, but the size of each frame is determined by the size of the overall image

No, that's not correct.
First of all, if you actually hire a pixel artist, you don't have to explain their workflow. They will figure it out, they know all of this stuff.
You can help them by providing as much example pictures as needed and explain what you like and don't like about them.
About the detail level.
The amount of pixels available in the final sprite determines the space for details. Don't mix up the amount of pixels with scaling of your assets. What you're actually looking at is this:
That is the actual canvas, those two artists had to work with.
If you draw something in 1000x1000px and shrink it down to 144x144px, there will be quality loss. An artist will have to do the actual pixel art work based on that. Not all artists work with a sketch, so leave it up to your artist. Just tell them, what you need.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
To help further clarify the language used here:
A pixel is a fixed size. Nothing is smaller than a pixel
(technically not true but for this matter that;s not important)
Resolution determines how many pixels are fit within that space. For example, your smart phone likely has a camera around 12 mega pixels, this means the images resolution would be 4243 pixels by 2828 pixels.
(again, let's not get into the weeds of what a mega pixel is)
Your picture 2 character appears to be 24 pixels tall. Meaning, without scaling the image up in size, that character would be able to fit into 1 smart phone image a few thousand times.
The reason why the image appears larger on your screen is because it's been scaled up.
Now, the SV sprite for RPG Maker has a larger resolution compared to the image 2 sprite you shared.
Finally, as previously mention is the color palette. Before old sprites were limited to a certain number of colors. 8 to 16 for the most popular eras of 2D games.
Today, such limitation does not exist. However to create the "pixel" feel, a limited color palette is necessary.
So you can tell your artist,
"I want you to make me a character with an x by x resolution, with a limited color palette."
Alternatively, like when I hired my artist, you can just say:
"I like your style, can you draw this character in that style? I'd like the character to be taller than (reference example  RTP sprite)"
